newsitem.title: JAPAN: Former copper king Hamanaka to go on trial soon.
newsitem.headline: Former copper king Hamanaka to go on trial soon.

text.p: One-time copper trading king Yasuo Hamanaka goes on trial on Monday, accused of masterminding a market swindle that became the biggest financial scandal in history.

The man who was once the most powerful figure in the world copper market but quiet and unassuming around friends and colleagues has made no public comment about the case since his arrest in October. His lawyers have refused to discuss their strategy.

"We"ve been worked hard for the trial, after receiving the prosecutor"s record (on questioning Hamanaka). But we don"t want to explain our strategy in advance," said Hidesato Sekine, one of a team of three lawyers.
Hamanaka is charged with forging documents and fraud, criminal offences that could bring him up to 15 years in prison.

Sekine said late last year that Hamanaka had admitted forgery and was keen to wrap up the trial quickly, although the lawyers have not indicated Hamanaka"s response to the more serious charge of fraud.
The case has reverberated far beyond Hamanaka, former employer Sumitomo Corp. and the $2.6 billion the company says he lost.

Like the Daiwa Bank scandal before it, the case has raised questions about Japan"s willingness to police its financial sector. Toshihide Iguchi, a Japanese-born bond trader who worked in Daiwa Bank"s New York office, was sentenced to four years in prison in December for hiding losses of $1.1 billion in unauthorised trades.
Before Sumitomo fired him last June, Hamanaka was known as "Mr Five Percent" since his trading team was believed to control nearly five percent of world copper trading.
Hamanaka was arrested last October 22 after Sumitomo filed a complaint accusing him of forging the documents that allowed him to open trading accounts.
Sumitomo said their employee of 26 years was solely to blame for racking up the losses from unauthorised trades.

Traders over the years have claimed that Hamanaka kept copper prices artificially high through skilful use of complex derivatives transactions and his iron grip on a large portion of copper stocks in London Metal Exchange warehouses.

He is being held at the Tokyo Detention House in eastern Tokyo, which is also holding another headline maker, Shoko Asahara, the cult guru who stands accused of plotting a poison gas attack on Tokyo"s subways in 1995.
Friends say that Hamanaka is holding up well in jail.
A former classmate at Seikei University, where he graduated in 1970, said: "I visited the detention house last December to see Hamanaka. He looked fine."

Aside from the criminal case, the whole affair is being investigated by regulators in Britain and the United States. Japanese financial regulators have repeatedly said that since the trades took place overseas, it has nothing to do with them.
A source close to the Tokyo prosecutor"s office said that Japan has given detailed records on its questioning of Hamanaka to overseas investigators.
Sumitomo, meanwhile, is silent on the trial and reiterated that its internal investigation is still going on.
"We"d like to finish the investigation as soon as possible, but cannot make comment on when," a Sumitomo spokesman said.
Sumitomo officials have repeatedly insisted Hamanaka was acting without his superiors" knowledge when he amassed the losses.
At one point the company claimed that it found no evidence their former star trader had manipulated the world market but asked about that recently, the Sumitomo spokesman said: "No comment."
